title: The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?
population: Conceptual model drawn mainly from team-sport athletes (no participants)
findings: Presents a 'training-injury prevention paradox': athletes accustomed to high training loads have fewer injuries than athletes training at lower workloads.

Cites evidence that team-sport athletes with more than 18 weeks of training before an initial injury were at reduced risk of a subsequent injury, and that high chronic workloads have been shown to decrease injury risk.
States that excessive and rapid increases in training load are likely responsible for a large proportion of non-contact soft-tissue injuries, and that under-training may increase injury risk.
Describes the acute:chronic workload ratio as a best-practice predictor of training-related injury (the author's claim, later critiqued).
limitations: Single-author narrative paper, not a systematic synthesis; team-sport focus; promotes ACWR, which later critiques (Impellizzeri 2020; Wang 2020) challenge; no running-specific data.
implications: Cutting load is not automatically protective: avoid drifting plans towards minimal volume for risk reasons, and prefer gradual build-up of chronic load.
Do not adopt its ACWR recommendation; use it only as the pro-ACWR counterweight to Impellizzeri 2020.

verification.notes: Added by verifier. Crossref: BJSM 50:273-280 (online Jan 2016), single author. Abstract read from Europe PMC (PMID 26758673).
